front: {{c1::Deindividuation}} = anonymity plus arousal and diffused responsibility, producing reduced self-awareness and disinhibited, group-norm-driven behavior.
why: Deindividuation is a named 7B group-process concept; discrete-question staple

front: {{c1::Kin selection}} explains helping relatives through inclusive fitness; {{c2::reciprocal altruism}} (Trivers) explains helping nonkin who can repay later.
why: Kin selection/inclusive fitness and reciprocal altruism are the AAMC altruism mechanisms

front: {{c1::Lowballing}} secures commitment and then raises the cost; {{c2::foot-in-the-door}} escalates from a small request via self-perception.
why: Compliance techniques (foot-in-the-door, lowball) are core 7B attitude/behavior change

front: {{c1::Self-handicapping}} means creating an obstacle in advance so that failure can be attributed {{c2::externally}} while success is credited doubly.
why: Self-handicapping is a secondary self-presentation concept; plausible but rarely decisive

front: {{c1::Social exchange}} theory says relationships persist when rewards exceed costs; {{c2::equity}} theory adds that being over-benefited also distresses.
why: Social exchange theory is on the AAMC outline; equity is its tested extension

front: A {{c1::stereotype}} is the cognitive belief about a group, {{c2::prejudice}} is the affective evaluation, and discrimination is the behavior.
why: Stereotype/prejudice/discrimination cognition-affect-behavior split is a high-frequency item

front: A cancer patient who compares herself with sicker patients feels better; comparing with healthier ones motivates but distresses. Name the theory.
why: Social comparison (up/down) is plausible passage context; not a frequent discrete point

front: A clinician reports egalitarian views yet shows faster pairing of one race with negative words on the IAT. What does this show, and what is the caveat?
why: Implicit vs explicit attitudes is tested; IAT psychometric caveat is second-step detail

front: A fundraiser first asks for a 500 dollar gift, is refused, then asks for 50 and gets it. Name the technique and its two mechanisms.
why: Door-in-the-face with reciprocal concession is a core compliance technique

front: A patient told firmly that he must quit smoking becomes more insistent on his right to smoke. Name the phenomenon and the counseling implication.
why: Reactance is a secondary persuasion concept; clinical framing is illustrative

front: Allport's contact hypothesis names four conditions under which contact reduces prejudice. What are they?
why: Contact hypothesis is testable; the four Allport conditions are supporting detail

front: Asch's effect was mostly {{c1::normative}} influence (public compliance, private disbelief); Sherif's autokinetic norms show {{c2::informational}} influence.
why: Normative vs informational social influence is a high-frequency distinction

front: At Robbers Cave, hostility between two boys' camps fell only when they had to repair a shared water supply. What theory and remedy does this illustrate?
why: Realistic conflict theory/superordinate goals are plausible; Robbers Cave is flavor

front: Berkowitz's revision: frustration causes aggression only via {{c1::negative affect}}, and aggressive cues such as guns ({{c2::the weapons effect}}) amplify it.
why: Frustration-aggression is tested; Berkowitz revision and weapons effect are secondary

front: Boys assigned to groups by a coin flip still allocated more money to their own group. Name the paradigm and the theory it supports.
why: Minimal group paradigm underpins social identity theory and in-group favoritism

front: Central-route persuasion requires both {{c1::motivation}} and {{c2::ability}} to elaborate, and it produces durable, behavior-predictive attitude change.
why: ELM central vs peripheral route is a core 7B attitude-change model

front: Cialdini's six principles of influence: reciprocity, commitment and consistency, {{c1::social proof}}, authority, liking, and {{c2::scarcity}}.
why: Cialdini's six principles are prep-book material, not AAMC outline; useful map

front: Dissonance can be reduced by changing the {{c1::behavior}}, changing or adding {{c2::cognitions}}, or trivializing the inconsistency.
why: Dissonance-reduction routes are supporting detail on the core dissonance card

front: Distinguish conformity, compliance, and obedience.
why: Conformity vs compliance vs obedience is a high-frequency distinction

front: Distinguish discrimination, prejudice, and ethnocentrism in social terms.
why: Prejudice/discrimination/ethnocentrism/relativism are core 8B definitions

front: Distinguish dispositional from situational attribution and the self-serving bias.
why: Dispositional vs situational attribution and self-serving bias are core 8B

front: Distinguish social facilitation from social loafing.
why: Social facilitation vs social loafing is a core 7B distinction

front: Festinger and Carlsmith (1959): what was the design, and which group changed its attitude?
why: Insufficient justification ($1 vs $20) is plausible passage material; study detail

front: Group polarization works through {{c1::persuasive arguments}} (hearing novel points favoring the lean) and {{c2::social comparison}} (outdoing the group norm).
why: Mechanisms of group polarization are second-step detail on a HIGH concept

front: Hamilton's rule: altruism toward kin evolves when {{c1::rB > C}}, the benefit weighted by genetic relatedness exceeding the cost to the helper.
why: Hamilton's rule is supporting detail on kin selection; formula itself rarely asked

front: How does Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis differ from egoistic accounts of helping?
why: Empathy-altruism vs egoistic helping is a plausible passage contrast; secondary

front: In Asch's variations, what most sharply reduced conformity?
why: Dissenter and group-size effects on conformity are plausible second-step points

front: In Bandura's 1965 follow-up, what did vicarious punishment change, and what did incentives reveal?
why: Learning vs performance in observational learning is testable; study detail

front: In ELM experiments, what variable flips people from peripheral to central processing?
why: Restates the ELM card: personal relevance is just the 'motivation' condition

front: In the {{c1::sleeper}} effect, a message from a discredited source gains influence over time because {{c2::source memory}} fades faster than the message.
why: Sleeper effect is not on the AAMC outline; named effect with little reasoning use

front: Kelley's covariation model: high {{c1::consensus}}, high {{c2::distinctiveness}}, and high consistency point to a situational (external) attribution.
why: Kelley's covariation model appears in prep and practice items; secondary to FAE

front: Latane and Darley's helping sequence: notice the event, {{c1::interpret it as an emergency}}, {{c2::take responsibility}}, know how to help, then act.
why: Five-step helping model and pluralistic ignorance are second-step bystander detail

front: Milgram obedience fell to about {{c1::30}}% with touch proximity and about {{c2::20}}% when the experimenter gave orders by phone.
why: Exact obedience percentages by variation are trivia; proximity effect suffices

front: Repeated, unreinforced exposure to a stimulus increases liking, an effect named {{c1::mere exposure}} and demonstrated by {{c2::Zajonc}}.
why: Mere exposure effect is a core attraction/persuasion mechanism

front: Same crowd, opposite effects: when does the presence of others improve versus worsen your performance?
why: Near-restatement of the facilitation/loafing and dominant-response cards

front: Stereotype threat impairs performance by loading {{c1::working memory}} with anxiety and monitoring; reduced by {{c2::self-affirmation}} and role models.
why: Stereotype threat mechanism/remedies are supporting detail on the core card

front: Subjects who guess a study's hypothesis behave so as to confirm it. Name this threat and the design features that control it.
why: Demand characteristics are tested research-methods content; misfiled here

front: Teachers told that certain randomly chosen students were late bloomers saw those students gain more on later testing. Name the effect and its mediator.
why: Restates the self-fulfilling prophecy card, which already names Pygmalion

front: The {{c1::actor-observer}} bias: we attribute our own behavior to the situation but others' identical behavior to their disposition.
why: Actor-observer bias is a high-frequency attribution distinction

front: The {{c1::halo}} effect spreads one positive trait to unrelated judgments; its mirror image is the {{c2::horns}} effect.
why: Halo effect is a frequently tested impression-formation bias

front: The {{c1::ultimate attribution error}} extends the FAE to groups: outgroup failures reflect disposition, outgroup successes reflect luck or special advantage.
why: Ultimate attribution error is a prep-book extension of FAE; secondary

front: The tendency to attribute others' behavior to disposition while excusing our own as situational is the {{c1::fundamental attribution error}} (with the {{c2::actor-observer}} asymmetry).
why: Restates the FAE card and the actor-observer card in one cloze

front: What are classic peripheral cues in persuasion, and when do they dominate?
why: Peripheral cues and when they dominate are supporting ELM detail

front: What are stereotype threat and the self-fulfilling prophecy?
why: Stereotype threat and self-fulfilling prophecy are core 8B concepts

front: What are the antecedents and hallmark symptoms of groupthink (Janis)?
why: Groupthink antecedents/symptoms are supporting detail on the core groupthink card

front: What are the key numbers from Asch's line-judgment conformity study?
why: Exact Asch percentages are trivia; the finding is on the plain Asch card

front: What are the main criticisms of Milgram's obedience studies?
why: Criticisms of Milgram and the Burger replication are discovery-history detail

front: What behavioral consequence does the just-world hypothesis predict?
why: Just-world hypothesis and victim blaming is a common discrete item

front: What biological correlates accompany aggression, and how do hostile and instrumental aggression differ?
why: Biological correlates and hostile vs instrumental aggression are plausible passage points

front: What did Asch's conformity study demonstrate?
why: Asch conformity/normative influence is core 7B

front: What did LaPiere's 1934 study show, and when do attitudes actually predict behavior?
why: Attitude-behavior consistency conditions are testable; LaPiere is flavor

front: What did Milgram's obedience study show?
why: Milgram obedience to authority is core 7B

front: What did Steele and Aronson's 1995 stereotype threat experiments show?
why: Study-history restatement of stereotype threat, already covered twice

front: What did Zimbardo's Stanford Prison Experiment illustrate?
why: Stanford Prison Experiment: social roles and situational power, core 7B

front: What factors increase interpersonal attraction?
why: Proximity, similarity, attractiveness, reciprocity are the tested attraction factors

front: What happened in the Stanford Prison Experiment, and why is it now heavily criticized?
why: SPE criticisms are discovery-history detail; the finding is on the plain SPE card

front: What is cognitive dissonance and how is it resolved?
why: Cognitive dissonance is core 7B attitude change

front: What is effort justification, and what is the classic evidence for it?
why: Effort justification is a plausible dissonance application; Aronson-Mills is flavor

front: What is group polarization and groupthink?
why: Group polarization and groupthink are core 7B group concepts

front: What is the bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility?
why: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility are core 7B

front: What is the difference between an in-group and out-group, and in-group bias?
why: In-group/out-group bias and out-group homogeneity are core 8B

front: What is the fundamental attribution error?
why: Fundamental attribution error is the most-tested attribution concept

front: What is the pattern and function of the self-serving bias, and when does it reverse?
why: Self-serving bias reversal in depression/collectivist cultures is second-step detail

front: What is the Ringelmann rope-pulling effect, and what conditions eliminate it?
why: Ringelmann effect restates social loafing with cultural/gender trivia

front: What were Milgram's baseline obedience findings?
why: The 65% headline figure is widely cited; supporting detail on the Milgram card

front: What were the key numbers in Darley and Latane's seizure (bystander) study?
why: Exact seizure-study percentages are trivia; bystander effect card covers it

front: What were the outcomes of Bandura's 1961 Bobo doll experiment?
why: Bobo doll observational learning of aggression is testable; details are secondary

front: When does Bem's self-perception theory explain attitude change better than dissonance theory?
why: Self-perception vs dissonance boundary is a plausible second-step item

front: Which situational factors increase helping, and what did the Good Samaritan seminary study show?
why: Situational helping factors are plausible passage context; Good Samaritan is flavor

front: Zajonc: an audience strengthens the {{c1::dominant}} response, improving {{c2::easy or well-learned}} tasks and impairing difficult ones.
why: Dominant-response mechanism of social facilitation is the tested explanation
